abstract:
Sanofi halted development of an oral STAT6 degrader that had been under study in a Phase I first-in-human trial in Europe. STAT6, a key drug target in type 2 inflammation, is among the five targets identified by the companies in their collaboration, launched in 2020.

The post StockWatch: Nurix Nosedives as Sanofi Halts Phase I Immunology Candidate appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Alex Philippidis

content.value:
Nurix Therapeutics (Nasdaq: NRIX) suffered its worst one-day loss as a public company Wednesday when Sanofi (Euronext Paris: SAN and Nasdaq: SNY) terminated development of the Phase I immunology candidate SAR448272 (NX-3911)—a key program of the companies’ nearly seven-year, up to $ 2.5 billion collaboration to discover, develop, and commercialize protein degradation drugs for “challenging” diseases.

The rest of the collaboration continues despite Sanofi pulling the plug on SAR448272 (NX-3911), an oral signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6) degrader that had been under study in a Phase I first-in-human trial in Europe (European Union Clinical Trials Register number 2026-526014-87-00). The trial began recruiting patients in Germany in July and had planned to expand recruitment into the Czech Republic, France, Italy, and Spain, a milestone that triggered a $10 million payment from Sanofi to Nurix in August.

STAT6, a key drug target in type 2 inflammation, is among the five targets identified by the companies in their collaboration, which took effect in January 2020 when Sanofi paid Nurix $55 million upfront. At the time, Sanofi committed to paying Nurix up to $2.5 billion in total payments, most of that tied to achieving research, preclinical, clinical, regulatory, and sales milestones.

As of August 31, Sanofi had paid Nurix a total $129 million—the $55 million upfront; $22 million in 2021 when Sanofi exercised an option to expand from three to five targets; $22 million for achieving research milestones; and $30 million for license extension fees—according to Nurix’s Form 10-Q quarterly report for the third quarter, filed October 13.

Nurix insisted that its recent cash runway guidance would not be affected by Sanofi’s halting development of SAR448272. Nurix said it had enough cash to fund operations into the second half of 2029 based on its $1.1 billion of cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities as of August 31.

Reassurance and rejection

“While [Tuesday]’s news is disappointing, Nurix remains in a strong position, with a substantial cash runway, three clinical-stage programs across our wholly owned and partnered portfolio, and an exciting preclinical pipeline,” Arthur T. Sands, MD, PhD, Nurix president and CEO, stated Tuesday after the close of markets.

The following day, investors appeared to reject that reassurance, selling off enough shares for Nurix stock to nosedive 38% from $25.82 to $15.95. Shares fell another 7% to $14.84 Thursday on a day the Nasdaq market had its worst one-day performance in the past 19 months—but the stock bounced back 3% Friday, finishing the week at $15.30 and a nearly 43% five-day decline.

“While we can understand the market’s knee-jerk disappointment following the news (STAT6 is regarded as a high-value target), we continue to view Nurix as a differentiated name within the emerging oral protein degrader space,” Tessa T. Romero, a senior analyst focused on biotechnology equity research with J.P. Morgan, wrote in a research note.

The reason why, Romero explained, is Nurix’s ongoing up-to-$2.3 billion global collaboration with Roche (SIX Swiss: RO and ROP) to develop bexobrutideg (“bexdeg” or “bexo”; NX-5948), a clinical-phase oral brain-penetrant Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) degrader.

In addition to the dollars, Romero said, that partnership is also attractive for Nurix because bexdeg can potentially be developed for numerous other therapeutic areas with diseases driven by BTK; the collaboration stretches across malignant hematology, immunology, and neurology.

Another reason why the Roche-Nurix partnership is attractive, the J.P. Morgan analyst added, is because Roche shoulders 60% of global development costs (with Nurix chipping in the other 40%) while the companies have agreed to split 50-50 both the U.S. commercialization responsibility (Roche holds sole ex-U.S. commercialization rights), as well as the resulting profits and losses from U.S. commercialization.

$48B market opportunity

“Historical stock moves around NRIX/STAT6 suggest the program carried some value, but was not the primary driver of NRIX’s value, with the much larger strategic inflection tied to the Roche/bexo partnership,” commented Roger Song, MD, equity analyst with Jefferies, in a research note.

In a June 8 investor presentation, Nurix quantified the size of that potential inflection as a $48 billion addressable market opportunity across five diseases: chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), and multiple sclerosis (MS).

CLL and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) are the two diseases where bex-deg development is furthest along; the drug is under study in the Phase III DAYBreak trial (CLL-306, NCT07516093), which is recruiting patients toward an estimated enrollment of 620, and carries an estimated primary completion date of October 2029. Last month, the first patient was enrolled in a Phase I/II combination trial (NX-5948-203; NCT07520006) evaluating the combination of bex-deg and venetoclax, a standard-of-care BCL2 inhibitor, in patients with relapsed/refractory CLL, with planned expansion to first-line therapy.

“We see opportunity for upside from bex-deg expansion into inflammatory/autoimmune and neurological indications,” Kostas Biliouris, PhD, a managing director on the biotechnology research team of Oppenheimer, wrote in a research note. “We see CSU as [a] particularly attractive indication given derisking of BTK-targeting by [Novartis’ (SIX Swiss: NOVN and NYSE: NVS) BTKi (BTK inhibitor)] remibrulnib and higher bex-deg potency on mast cell degranulation assay without bleeding risk.

Sanofi’s decision

So why did Sanofi terminate development of SAR448272?

Nurix offered no reason in its press release, and company executives told Song of Jefferies it was not told in advance of the decision.

“The decision was due to emerging nonclinical findings that precluded Sanofi from bringing it forward in atopic dermatitis,” Sanofi indicated to Nurix during a quick catch up conversation, according to Romero, who cautioned: “Nurix has not reviewed any data and therefore could not confirm the issues Sanofi saw. Nurix is also unclear whether Sanofi’s broader portfolio strategy played a role in the decision.”

Biliouris offered a possible portfolio explanation for Sanofi’s decision: “It may be driven by robust/convincing (HV) data from other SNY [Sanofi] collaboration (STAT6i), STAT6 degrader safety signals, or SNY strategic prioritization following [Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (Nasdaq: REGN)]’s partnership around long-acting IL-13/IL-13 x IL-14,” Biliouris wrote.

Sanofi is partnering with privately held Recludix Pharma to develop an oral STAT6 inhibitor or “STAT6i” called REX-8756 (also known as SAR448755). REX-8756 is a first-in-class, reversible orthosteric inhibitor of the STAT6 SH2 domain that targets Type 2 inflammatory pathways (IL-4 and IL-13), and which according to the companies is designed to be highly potent, selective, and durable.

The companies have advanced REX-8756 to a Phase I trial designed to assess the drug’s safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics, with single ascending dose (SAD) and multiple ascending dose (MAD) cohorts. The blinded, placebo-controlled trial expects to enroll approximately 100 healthy volunteers.

Recludix presented positive preclinical model data for REX-856 at the Revolutionizing Atopic Dermatitis (RAD) Congress, held June 17-19 in Nashville, TN. Sanofi and Recludix launched their collaboration in 2023. It includes $125 million in “near-term” payments; up to $1.2 billion-plus in development, regulatory and sales milestones; as well as up to double-digit royalties on product sales.

More recently last month, Sanofi and Regeneron expanded their 23-year-old partnership—whose most successful product is the multi-indication blockbuster Dupixent® (dupilumab)—by adding multiple next-generation, long-acting antibodies to their alliance. Sanofi agreed to pay Regeneron $1 billion upfront, and up to an additional $7 billion tied to achieving development, regulatory, and commercial milestones.

Under the expanded license and collaboration agreement, Sanofi and Regeneron agreed to co-develop and co-commercialize four new long-acting, Regeneron-invented antibodies targeting interleukin-13 (IL-13), IL-4xIL-13 bispecific, interleukin-4 (IL-4), and interleukin-4 receptor alpha (IL-4Rα). The IL-13 antibody, REGN20423, is now being evaluated in the Phase I AURA-AD trial (NCT07527923) in atopic dermatitis, while the other three antibodies are expected to enter the clinic in 2027.

 

Leaders and laggards

Karyopharm Therapeutics (KPTI) shares skidded 21% Tuesday, from 11 cents to 9 cents, after the Newton, MA-based developer of nuclear export inhibitors designed to treat cancer said it filed for protection from creditors under Chapter 11 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas. Karyopharm said it entered into a Restructuring Support Agreement with its lenders, noteholders, and other key stakeholders, under which the company, once reorganized, plans to merge with privately held, London-based Ayrmid—which has agreed to serve as lead bidder in a court-supervised sale process intended to maximize value for all stakeholders. Karyopharm said it has secured commitments for up to $55 million in debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing from its existing secured lenders. Upon court approval, the DIP financing plus cash from ongoing operations is expected to support Karyopharm operations during the Chapter 11 process and meet the company’s financial obligations.

Rhythm Pharmaceuticals (NASDAQ: RYTM) shares surged 28% from $86.44 to $110.68 Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that AstraZeneca (LSE, NYSE, and Nasdaq Stockholm: AZN) made a roughly $10 billion offer to buy the rare disease drug developer, citing unnamed sources. AstraZeneca offered to pay $124 a share for the biotech last month, the Journal reported—a 35% premium over Rhythm’s closing share price Tuesday. AstraZeneca raised its bid to $134 a share, according to Reuters. Rhythm has declined comment while AstraZeneca has not commented on the reported offers. Shares slid 5% to $105.02 Thursday before rising again 7% to $112.28 Friday, after the merger-and-acquisition blog Betaville posted speculation from traders that a second potential global pharma giant may have made a counteroffer for Rhythm.
